Because Chinese medicine in antiquity had no anatomy, the term "sciatica" did not exist. As with other pain, traditional Chinese medicine attributes it to invasion by "Wind-Cold-Damp" pathogens, which lodge in the meridians and cause congealing and stagnation of Qi and Blood.

From the Chinese-medicine perspective, sciatica belongs to the category of "Bi syndrome" (painful obstruction), especially related to "lumbar-leg pain" and "sinew Bi." Its core pathomechanism is obstruction of the meridians with Qi and Blood stasis — "where there is no free flow, there is pain" — while at the same time being closely related to dysfunction of the Zang-Fu organs.

Analyzed from the Zang-Fu perspective, the root of sciatica is commonly associated with the following organ dysfunctions and invasion by the six external pathogens:

Decline of Kidney Qi and insufficiency of Liver Blood (the fundamental internal cause): Chinese medicine holds that the Kidney governs bone and stores Essence — when Kidney Qi is depleted, the bone marrow is not replenished and the lumbar vertebrae lose nourishment, leading to disc degeneration and bony proliferation that compress the nerve roots (corresponding to structural problems in Western medicine such as lumbar disc herniation). The Liver governs the sinews and stores Blood — when Liver Blood is insufficient, the sinews lose their moistening nourishment, becoming stiff and inelastic, prone to injury and contracture, and pulling on or compressing the nerve.

Liver and Kidney share a common source: After middle age, Liver and Kidney Essence and Blood naturally decline, forming the internal basis for this disease. Manifestations include soreness and weakness of the lumbar region and knees, aversion to cold or vexation and insomnia, dizziness, and tinnitus. Spleen Deficiency with exuberant Dampness, Phlegm and stasis obstructing the collaterals (the key precipitating factor).

The Spleen governs the muscles and the transformation of water-damp: Prolonged sitting, physical overwork, or dietary irregularity damages Spleen Qi, producing muscular weakness; the core muscle groups (especially of the lumbar-abdominal region) lose nourishment and cannot stabilize the lumbar spine, increasing the structural burden.

Internal generation of turbid Dampness: Spleen Deficiency generates Dampness, which is heavy, turbid, and sticky by nature. Turbid Dampness pours into the meridians of the lower back and legs, obstructing the Qi dynamic, and combines with Cold or Heat to form Cold-Damp or Damp-Heat — the direct pathological factor producing pain, heaviness, and numbness.

Invasion by external pathogens with blockage of the collaterals (the direct external cause): When the Zang-Fu are deficient, the defensive exterior is unconsolidated, and external pathogens such as Wind, Cold, Dampness, and Heat easily invade through the deficiency, obstructing the meridians of the lumbar region and lower limbs.

Cold-Damp congealing and stagnation: Cold-Damp most readily causes sciatica; this pain is severe, aggravated by cold and slightly relieved by warmth, with heaviness of the limbs.

Damp-Heat pouring downward: Damp-Heat can also cause sciatica, with burning-type pain, possible local heat, scanty dark urine, and a yellow, greasy tongue coating.

Understanding sciatica from the perspective of the Zang-Fu and the six external pathogens

To analyze a pain, the most direct method is to examine the location of the pain and ask which "meridian" abnormality is responsible. The pain in the cutaneous sensory territory supplied by the sciatic nerve involves the lumbar region, buttock, posterior and lateral thigh, posterolateral lower leg, and lateral foot.

Based on these locations, if one examines the meridians of the buttock on an acupuncture bronze figure, it is clear that the routes are those of the Gallbladder meridian and the Bladder meridian — abnormality of these two meridians is the cause.

Bladder Meridian of Foot-Taiyang (the principal pathway): Its course "runs alongside the spine to reach the lumbar region, enters along the paraspinal muscles, and connects with the Kidney... a branch descends from the lumbar region alongside the spine, passes through the buttock, and enters the popliteal fossa... another branch passes through the hip pivot, follows the posterolateral aspect of the thigh, joins in the popliteal fossa, and then passes down through the calf..." Corresponding to the body, the route runs from the lumbar region along the posterior buttock, the midline of the posterior thigh, and the posterior lower leg down to the foot. This is the most common pain pathway in sciatica (a Taiyang meridian pattern).

Gallbladder Meridian of Foot-Shaoyang (the secondary pathway): Its course "runs along the neck in front of the Hand-Shaoyang meridian to the top of the shoulder... descends into the axilla, follows the chest, passes the free ribs, and joins at the hip pivot; from there it follows the lateral thigh, emerges at the lateral aspect of the knee, and descends in front of the fibula..." Corresponding to the body, pain radiates from the buttock along the lateral thigh and lateral lower leg to the lateral dorsum of the foot (a Shaoyang meridian pattern).

In addition, the Stomach Meridian of Foot-Yangming and the Spleen Meridian of Foot-Taiyin are involved when there is numbness or muscular atrophy of the anterior or medial lower leg, related to insufficient nourishment by the Qi and Blood of the Spleen and Stomach meridians.

The "Gallbladder meridian" and "Bladder meridian" of modern people show year-round Qi stagnation and Blood stasis

Large volumes of meridian data from modern people show that the Gallbladder and Bladder meridians take turns being obstructed in virtually all four seasons (see figure below).

The Gallbladder meridian shows a Deficiency pattern throughout the year, its energy falling lower as the weather gets colder; while the Bladder meridian's energy drops sharply after May, falling lower the hotter the weather becomes.

In summer the pain is triggered by the Bladder meridian; in winter by the Gallbladder meridian

Therefore, from the perspective of meridian energy, both hot summers and cold winters are seasons in which sciatica readily occurs: in summer the pain is provoked by the Bladder meridian, in winter by the Gallbladder meridian — the two "brothers" cooperating perfectly.

In terms of meridian patterns, in summer Bladder meridian obstruction presents as the Iron Triangle meridian combination, while in winter it appears as a joint Deficiency pattern together with the Stomach meridian.

Add to this the fact that modern people generally sit for long periods without exercise: whether or not there is buttock pain, the Qi and Blood of the buttocks remain in a state of prolonged stagnation. Once the Qi-Blood obstruction has persisted long enough, sciatica appears, and it is no surprise that the pain extends to the thigh.

The meridians leading to the human buttock are severely obstructed in Qi and Blood in virtually all four seasons

From the perspective of meridian interconnection, the Stomach meridian must also be added

From the analysis above, judging by the meridians leading to the buttock, sciatica should simply be the result of impaired Qi-Blood flow in the "Gallbladder meridian" and "Bladder meridian."

However, large volumes of meridian data show that the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians are highly interlinked and usually present Deficiency patterns together, more severely the colder the weather. Adding these three meridians together, it can be said that the Yang meridians of modern people's legs are deficient in Qi and Blood all year round.

Taking 2021 as an example, a female member shared that after entering winter she began to experience pain in the lumbar region and buttock, extending to the thigh and the back of the knee.

She continuously observed her body's meridian phenomena and found that they were indeed as published in Cloud TCM's articles: simultaneous Deficiency patterns of the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Kidney meridians.

In winter, when the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians show Deficiency patterns, sciatica readily appears

Because the Gallbladder meridian connects to the Dai (Girdle) Vessel at the waist, and its energy is low in the cold winter, accompanied by low energy of the Stomach and Kidney meridians, pain resembling sciatica readily appears, with the pain distributed over the lumbar region, buttock, lateral thigh and lower leg, and lateral foot.

Over the past several years, members have frequently reported sciatica. In 2026, statistics on several hundred sciatica meridian patterns showed concentration mainly in the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" and the "composite meridian pattern," both dominated by Deficiency of the Bladder or Gallbladder meridian, confirming that the ancient theory is genuine.

Common meridian patterns in sciatica

Sciatica can also appear in the hot summer

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that invasion of the body by "Wind-Cold-Damp" pathogens readily causes various Bi pains, so winter is the most severe season; yet summer is also hard to escape, and meridian assessment can confirm this phenomenon.

The "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" mentioned above appears most readily in the hot summer — meaning that sciatica can also occur in summer.

For example, one member began meridian assessments in October 2019 (winter), at which time his meridian pattern showed Deficiency of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians. At that time, aside from occasional shoulder soreness and upper back pain, he had never experienced buttock pain.

However, after June 2020, in summer, when average temperatures in Taiwan exceeded 38°C and the outdoor temperature was above body temperature, he gradually developed spasmodic pain in the buttock extending down the entire back of the thigh; it throbbed when he sat in a chair, his gait felt odd, the pain sometimes extended into the leg, and his calf would sometimes cramp.

The winter Deficiency pattern of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians had almost completely disappeared by summer

He went to hospital for X-ray examination; the physician told him no skeletal or disc herniation abnormality was found, so with no clear cause identified he could only undergo rehabilitation. He reasoned that this should still fall within the domain of the meridians and began studying his own meridian data.

Comparing the meridian phenomena of those two months from his assessments, he discovered that in winter he had shown Gallbladder and Stomach meridian Deficiency, whereas in summer the Bladder meridian instead became severely deficient while the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians returned to normal. Thus his sciatica appeared in summer rather than winter.

When this member was interviewed again in 2026, he shared that after five years of expelling Cold, his sciatica had disappeared — had this case not been recorded, he would have forgotten he had sciatica years earlier.

The principle of meridian correspondence and sciatica

Cloud TCM's methods of improving pain frequently draw on the principle of meridian correspondence, and sciatica is no exception.

As noted above, the "three Yang meridians" of the leg are the culprits of sciatica. Based on the Zang-Fu Bie Tong (organ-pairing) Yin-Yang correspondence principle, acupoints for improving sciatica can also be found on the "three Yin meridians" of the arm.

By correspondence, massaging the meridians of the arm can also improve sciatica

Commonly used points include Yuji (LU-10), Chize (LU-5), and Shaohai (HT-3), all with very good effect.

Since sciatica clearly arises from abnormality of the three Yang meridians of the leg, directly massaging or patting the Bladder, Gallbladder, and Stomach meridians is the most straightforward approach.

If one adds patting of the three arm meridians, locating the painful spots and reinforcing with patting, gua sha, cupping, and so on, then once the Qi-Blood obstruction is removed, even severe sciatica will improve by more than half.

This correspondence method is often unfathomably profound and repeatedly achieves remarkable results. For example, one member with sciatica once consulted a Chinese medicine practitioner skilled in Master Tung's extraordinary points; after the practitioner needled Linggu and Dabai, the pain disappeared completely within 30 seconds, to his delighted astonishment.

Linggu and Dabai treat buttock and lower-limb pain with rapid effect

Why can needling the hand improve buttock pain? This is the mysterious aspect of Chinese medicine. These points, however, work better with acupuncture; finger-pressure fails to bring out their remarkable efficacy, so professional assistance with needling is required to obtain results.

Improving the meridian constitution is the fundamental method

Cloud TCM constantly emphasizes one key point: no matter how miraculous and effective a treatment may be, even if it can eliminate pain in seconds, if no effort is made to improve the meridian constitution, the problem will recur someday in the future.

Therefore, what Cloud TCM promotes is long-term observation of one's own meridian constitution and diligent work to improve and balance one's meridians, which allows clear and definite disease prevention. So-called "cure" is only a temporary phenomenon; without improving the constitution, recurrence lies ahead.

When a person's constitution is very Cold, upon entering winter the energy of the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Kidney meridians becomes extremely low and the Qi-Blood state weak, readily producing so-called "Bi pain" — and this is how sciatica arises.

When a person lives under prolonged stress and accumulated fatigue and develops the rigid, unchanging "Iron Triangle meridian pattern," with the Bladder meridian's energy low in all four seasons, they can hardly escape the grip of sciatica — all of which is entirely predictable and preventable.

On this basis, improving the body's Cold-Heat state through Chinese herbal medicine or food is also a good method. The classical-formula expert known as Uncle JT once noted that Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang (Ephedra, Aconite and Asarum Decoction) plus Shao Yao Gan Cao Tang (Peony and Licorice Decoction) is the most commonly used structure for improving sciatica.

Through the practical experience of many Cloud TCM members over more than 10 years, it has been confirmed that Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang is definitively effective in expelling Wind-Cold from the body and relieving pain. Shao Yao Gan Cao Tang is also known as the "Cane-Discarding Decoction"; combined, their effect in improving leg disorders is trustworthy.

Improving lifestyle habits (e.g., not staying up late, resting when tired) and dress (e.g., wearing long trousers, not exposing the navel, not wearing high heels) are also fundamental methods of improving the meridian constitution.

Note 1: Master Tung's extraordinary points on the hand — Zhongbai, Xiabai, Wanshun 1 and 2, Yunbai, Libai, Shangqu, Xiaqu, Jianzhong (Shoulder Center), and Jianzhong (Establish Center) — all have remarkable effects.

"Sciatica" is a considerably distressing pain. Some say sciatica is not a disease, yet when it flares it is unbearable: during an attack the patient cannot sit, stand, or lie down comfortably, and cannot sleep at night, causing enormous suffering.

The sciatic nerve arises near the 4th–5th lumbar spinal nerves and is the longest peripheral nerve in the human body. When it is compressed, pain or aching numbness extends from the lower back to the buttock, the thigh (lateral or posterior aspect), the lower leg (posterior, anterolateral, or anteromedial aspect), the dorsum of the foot, or the sole. It may occur in only one leg, or both legs may be painful.

Besides pain in these regions, impairments of bodily movement appear, such as inability to bend forward or sit down, difficulty walking, weakness of both legs, asymmetry in lower-body muscle bulk between the two sides, and dulled sensation in the feet.

According to modern medical statistics, as many as 60–80% of Taiwanese people have experienced low back and buttock pain, with similar incidence in men and women; overseas statistics put the incidence of sciatica at 10–40%, showing that it is a common symptom.

Strictly speaking, sciatica is only a "symptom" rather than a disease; it is usually caused by other problems or disorders.

The most common site of sciatic nerve compression is the lumbar spine, where common causes include compression of the vertebrae (e.g., lumbar spondylosis, bone spurs, disc herniation, lumbar spondylolisthesis, tumor, tuberculosis) or muscular compression (piriformis syndrome).

Because the cause is spinal compression, modern medicine can confirm the diagnosis with X-ray, myelography, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging.

Treatment consists of bed rest, muscle relaxants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, wearing a back brace, pelvic traction, rehabilitation therapy, or radiotherapy; severe cases require surgical treatment such as discectomy or vertebrectomy.

If these scientific investigations fail to identify a clear cause, or if treatment is ineffective and surgery is not desired, the Chinese-medicine mode of thinking can then be considered and may offer a new line of approach.

Neck pain and wry neck have troubled the Chinese people for over a thousand years. The ancients called it "neck-nape pain," dividing the neck into front and back parts: the front called "jing" (neck) and the back called "xiang" (nape).

The Huangdi Neijing states: "For great Wind with neck-nape pain, needle Fengfu (GV-16)." The discussion here mainly concerns the "nape," that is, the posterior and lateral parts of the neck.

To understand neck pain and wry neck from Chinese medicine, the simplest method is to apply meridian theory. The meridians running to the back of the neck are the same as those running to the shoulder and neck — six meridians in total.

These meridians are: the Bladder meridian, Gallbladder meridian, Sanjiao meridian, Large Intestine meridian, Small Intestine meridian, and the Du (Governing) Vessel, including among the Extraordinary Vessels the Yang Qiao (Yang Motility) and Yang Wei (Yang Linking) Vessels.

The meridians affecting the neck are principally six

Knowing which meridians are associated with neck pain, one can, by observing meridian data, discern the relationship between the meridians and wry neck. The main possibilities are as follows:

1. External Cold Damage and Wind-Cold invasion

The most common cause of neck pain is "externally contracted Cold Damage." As far back as the Han-dynasty Shanghan Lun it is stated: "In Taiyang disease, with stiffness of the nape and back, no sweating, and aversion to wind, Ge Gen Tang (Kudzu Decoction) governs it."

So-called Taiyang disease is closely bound to the Bladder Meridian of Foot-Taiyang. That is, after contracting external Wind-Cold, the Qi and Blood of the Bladder meridian readily become abnormal, producing neck soreness or wry neck.

Wry neck appears most readily during externally contracted Cold Damage

In early May 2023, Taiwan had already become generally hot, but on some days the temperature suddenly dropped by more than 10°C. A member went out to work in the morning wearing short sleeves, finding it pleasantly cool at the time.

By evening, walking along the street after work, the wind was strong and she felt very cold, having brought no extra clothing. She thought she could simply endure it and thought nothing of it.

The next morning she woke with a wry neck and severe pain. Having studied a little Chinese herbal medicine, she immediately took Ge Gen Tang, and within two days the wry neck improved.

A common cold has no fixed meridian pattern, but since the regions leading to the shoulder and neck are served entirely by Yang meridians, contracting external Wind-Cold lowers the energy of the Yang meridians and produces neck pain — this is the most common cause of wry neck.

2. Deficiency patterns of the Spleen and Bladder meridians

From the meridians related to the neck it can be seen that the Du Vessel and the Bladder meridian are the principal channels governing the entire back of the neck.

Large volumes of meridian data from modern people show that Bladder meridian Deficiency (insufficiency of Qi and Blood) is a persistent and common meridian phenomenon in modern people, and with it the Du Vessel's Qi-Blood flow also becomes obstructed.

One of the common meridian constitutions of modern people with frequent neck pain

The data also show high interconnection between the Spleen and Bladder meridians: when the Bladder meridian is deficient, the Spleen meridian is deficient as well. Through the Zang-Fu Bie Tong (organ-pairing) interconnection, this is reflected onto the Small Intestine meridian, which likewise produces neck pain.

This meridian phenomenon becomes especially pronounced after entering summer, and in some people appears stably in all four seasons. Because it looks like a triangle, it is called the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern."

Member Mr. C is a computer engineer. Because of chronic poor working posture, his entire back, shoulders, and neck were as hard as stone, with frequent shoulder-neck soreness and no idea what to do about it.

He said: "My shoulders and neck have been treated to ruin! Acupuncture, cupping, tuina, and massage everywhere have all stopped working — the muscles of my whole back are fibrotic!" His meridian charts regularly showed this phenomenon.

Modern medicine has found that "stress" is frequently the chief cause of neck pain, and after stress or staying up late, the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" quickly appears.

Therefore, those under great stress or who often stay up late most readily develop this meridian phenomenon — no wonder stress produces neck pain or wry neck. The secret is thus unlocked![@ad:1]

3. Deficiency patterns of the three hand Yang meridians

From the meridian bronze-figure of channels leading to the neck it is clear that the three hand Yang meridians (Large Intestine, Sanjiao, and Small Intestine) travel to the neck. Extensive observation of members has likewise found: whenever any one of these three meridians — or all of them — presents a Deficiency pattern, the neck and shoulders are invariably tight.

Meridian phenomena prone to neck pain

Modern people pursue empirical verification, and in fact anyone can verify this themselves: sleep naked at night in front of an electric fan or air conditioner, giving the body's Yang Qi no protection whatsoever and letting Cold invade the body — the next day, pain will begin in the neck, shoulders, and the neck-shoulder junction, possibly to the point of being unable to turn the head.

In summer, people love drinking iced water. Since these three meridians all ultimately travel to the abdomen, a damp and cold abdomen also produces shoulder-neck soreness; simply drinking large amounts of iced water reproduces this experience, and most people will certainly "succeed."

Since everyone's Gallbladder meridian is severely deficient in winter, as the meridian chart above shows, anyone who does not develop shoulder-neck soreness in winter can be counted as having abundant Yang Qi and very good health.

4. Wind-Cold-Damp invading the body

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that when "Wind-Damp" invades the body, neck pain appears most readily — simply put, the neck pain of a common cold. Hence the ancients would prescribe Dampness-dispelling and Wind-dispelling herbs to treat neck pain, with a certain degree of effect.

The great majority of modern people, not knowing how to deal with Wind-Cold and Wind-Damp within the body, take only antibiotics when they catch a cold, leaving the meridians in a long-term state of obstruction.

Stress by day, staying up late by night, muscles held tense — after many years of this, an extremely refractory neck pain can be forged.

Refractory shoulder-neck pain requires many years of accumulated "cultivation" to form

For such refractory neck pain, beyond dispelling Wind, dispelling Cold, and dispelling stasis, the adhesions between the various muscles must be kneaded apart — and not only around the neck; one must also relax from within the mind before the muscles can truly release. It is unquestionably a major undertaking.

Why is neck pain so often a symptom of major disease? Looking at the meridian chart above makes it clear: when a person's Qi-Blood circulation is poor over the long term and the Bladder meridian is chronically deficient, the Qi and Blood of the meridians that ultimately reach the brain are perpetually insufficient — so the eventual appearance of "stroke" is no surprise.

Observation of the meridian patterns of stroke in some members clearly shows that, indeed, the Bladder meridian is always deficient. Therefore, beginning health cultivation when neck pain is still mild is a basic discipline for preventing stroke and various major diseases — a quite definite warning signal for prevention.

The simplest ways to prevent and improve shoulder-neck soreness are: get adequate sleep; frequently relax the muscles around the shoulders and neck from the "mind" outward, or regularly perform some simple exercises; and at the same time do not let the shoulder-neck region get chilled or be blown on directly by wind.

When shoulder-neck soreness occurs, applying moxibustion, a hot hair dryer, or far-infrared irradiation directly to the area is the fastest and simplest way to improve it.

Everything was fine yesterday, yet this morning you wake to find your neck so painful that you cannot turn it up, down, left, or right. Stiff neck pain extends into the shoulder and neck muscles, and all you can say to family and friends is: "I've got a wry neck!"

"Wry neck" (stiff neck on waking) is essentially a colloquial term; in modern medical terminology it is called "acute painful torticollis," "acute periarthritis of the cervical joints," "cervical muscle sprain," and so on.

What puzzles many people is: if one has merely been lying quietly all night during sleep, how could an acute sprain and inflammation appear so suddenly the next day?

There are many causes of neck soreness. Modern medicine regards wry neck as an acute strain of the cervical muscles, usually caused primarily by a problem with the "pillow" or the "sleeping posture."

"Stress" is frequently a principal cause of wry neck. Modern statistics find that most people with habitual wry neck are those who readily put excessive pressure on themselves, with traits including Type A personality, proneness to tension, perfectionism, and an excessive drive to do well.

Any posture that produces long-term tension of the back, head, and shoulder-neck musculature can cause chronic neck pain.

Modern people use mobile phones and computers for long periods, and "heads-down" users are ever more numerous. Bending the head 60 degrees to look at a phone places great pressure on the neck, so wry neck has also been called "text neck."

Poor posture at the computer keeps muscles tense and produces adhesions of the back muscles.

Chronic neck pain is most likely after motor-vehicle trauma; chronic neck pain may well be "cervical degenerative arthritis," the degenerative arthritis of advancing age occurring in the neck.

If a cervical disc herniates and bone spurs form, the result is not merely neck pain but also arm numbness and pain, headache, and other manifestations of cervical spondylosis.

Some serious diseases such as meningitis, epiglottitis, stroke, myocardial infarction, and malignant tumors can also present with neck pain. Therefore, when modern medicine treats neck pain, structural bone disease and other diseases must first be excluded.

For simple acute wry neck, heat application can first be used to ease the pain, along with anti-inflammatory analgesics and muscle relaxants, combined with physical therapy — this is the typical modern medical approach.

Chinese medicine has more than a thousand years of clinical experience treating neck pain, so most people, when a wry neck suddenly appears, seek out Chinese medicine, acupoints, or massage as complementary therapies; since the results have consistently been good, they are worthy of trust.

Pain of the shoulder joint and the surrounding muscles and sinews producing "inability to raise the shoulder," a Wind-Damp disorder, has troubled the Chinese people for thousands of years. As far back as the Huangdi Neijing and the Zhenjiu Jiayi Jing (Systematic Classic of Acupuncture and Moxibustion), this symptom was already discussed, so the similar terms are extremely numerous; in antiquity it belonged to the category of "Bi syndrome" (painful obstruction).

Shoulder pain is not limited to frozen shoulder. A person may experience transient shoulder joint pain as early as age 20, and shoulder joint pain seldom appears alone: it often extends to the upper back and scapula as "back pain," and also into the upper arm as "shoulder-arm pain." This can be understood easily through the meridians.

As is customary, to explore shoulder joint pain one must first understand which meridians travel to the shoulder joint. In fact, all the meridians of the arm travel to the shoulder joint, as the figure below clearly shows. Thus if any one of these six meridians suffers decades of meridian Qi-Blood obstruction, frozen shoulder can result. Is this analysis not simple?

The meridians passing through the shoulder joint are actually numerous and complex

That being so, in the 30 years before frozen shoulder appears — that is, at around age 20 — which meridian abnormalities most readily arise to produce shoulder joint pain? There are three groups:

1. The Taiyang meridians (Small Intestine and Bladder)

The Taiyang meridians (Small Intestine and Bladder) are the most easily obstructed, with obstruction beginning even before age 10. The reason is simple: from a person's first cold in life onward, the Taiyang meridians begin to be obstructed, because according to the Han-dynasty Shanghan Lun, externally contracted Cold Damage invades the Taiyang meridians first.

The Taiyang meridians guard the body's most vital back and heart

The figure above shows clearly that the Taiyang meridians guard the body's most important regions — the back and the heart. When the Taiyang meridians are abnormal, all the locations marked with red lines can become painful: the upper and lower arm, shoulder joint, scapula, and the entire back. Understood this way, it becomes very easy.

Because Taiyang-stage disease resolves spontaneously, a 20-year-old pays it no mind, and continues to ignore it at ages 30–40. Imperceptibly, the muscles and fascia along these meridians have already begun to form adhesions. Then one day at 50 he discovers: "Eh? Why can't I suddenly lift my arm?"

2. Deficiency patterns of the Large Intestine and Sanjiao meridians

Large volumes of meridian data from modern people show that the Sanjiao and Large Intestine meridians are close brothers whose energies regularly move together, usually in Excess patterns. However, in a certain proportion of people these two meridians present Deficiency patterns — decidedly bad news for the shoulder joint.

When the Sanjiao and Large Intestine meridians are deficient, shoulder-neck soreness readily appears

Why does this phenomenon occur? It too is related to the common cold — this may be what traditional Chinese medicine calls "Warm disease," most severe in early spring each year. The deep Cold accumulated through the winter is discharged as the weather warms, at which point cold symptoms appear.

Because the Qi and Blood of the Sanjiao and Large Intestine meridians leading to the shoulder are severely insufficient, shoulder-neck soreness readily appears at this time, and shoulder joint pain becomes hard to avoid.

3. Simultaneous Deficiency of the three hand Yin meridians (Lung, Heart, and Pericardium)

Many Cloud TCM members have found, after performing their own meridian assessments, the phenomenon of the three hand Yin meridians (Lung, Heart, and Pericardium) presenting Deficiency patterns together — and not just once, but frequently. This clearly indicates chronic obstruction of Qi and Blood in these three meridians.

Deficiency of the three hand Yin meridians (Lung, Heart, and Pericardium): the colder the weather, the higher the probability

The probability of this meridian phenomenon likewise rises as the weather gets colder. Thus in winter, a certain proportion of people have clearly insufficient Qi and Blood in the region leading to the anterior shoulder joint, readily producing shoulder joint pain, together with chest oppression, chest pain, heart pain — even possible myocardial infarction.

Based on the above, viewed from the Chinese-medicine angle of the "six external pathogens," frozen shoulder arises because the body has contracted "Wind-Cold" or "Dampness," causing chronic obstruction of the body's meridians; the sinew channels (muscles) lack nourishment, and only after very, very many years of brewing and accumulation do severe adhesions appear, culminating in an arm that cannot be raised. Hence certain Chinese herbal formulas improve shoulder pain specifically by dispelling Wind-Cold and Dampness (e.g., Er Zhu Tang and Qiang Huo Sheng Shi Tang).

From the standpoint of Chinese medicine's meridians, frozen shoulder takes a very long accumulation to form

From the Chinese-medicine angle of "Zang-Fu Qi and Blood," frozen shoulder arises because chronic fatigue produces Qi-Blood insufficiency, Spleen-Stomach weakness, dual Deficiency of Liver and Kidney, and other disharmonies of the five Zang and six Fu; after many, many years of brewing and accumulation, all the meridians and sinew channels leading to the shoulder become blocked (Qi stagnation and Blood stasis). Hence certain Chinese herbal formulas improve shoulder pain specifically by tonifying Qi, nourishing Blood, supplementing Liver and Kidney, and dispelling Blood stasis (e.g., Ba Zhen Tang, Liu Wei Di Huang Wan, and Shen Tong Zhu Yu Tang).

Examining the meridian phenomena of fifty-year-olds directly

All the above are meridian phenomena that can produce shoulder joint pain. Since the topic here is "fifty-year shoulder," would it not be simplest and most direct to observe the meridian phenomena of people aged 50? The meridian charts below show the two most common meridian patterns of people over 50.

People over 50 generally have insufficient energy in the leg meridians

From the meridian charts of those over 50 it can be seen that almost not a single meridian in the whole body is normal. To put it in one sentence: in many people past 50, whether viewed from the meridians or from the sinew channels (muscles), the shoulder region is simply a wretched, chaotic mess.

Modern medical research finds that diabetic patients develop frozen shoulder at 2–4 times the rate of the general population; 80% of stroke patients develop shoulder soreness; many frozen-shoulder patients learn only at the hospital that they have cardiovascular disease; thyroid disease patients very readily develop frozen shoulder; and quite a few patients with hepatobiliary inflammation develop right shoulder pain.

By remarkable coincidence, the two meridian patterns above are precisely the meridian constitution patterns frequently seen in patients with diabetes, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, Parkinson's disease, stroke, hypertension, and hepatobiliary disease.

Readers of other Cloud TCM articles know that the meridians correspond with one another, so abnormalities of the leg meridians also affect the arms. This is why people over 50 are more prone to shoulder joint pain, and even pain in other parts of the body.

Many readers at this point will say: "Nonsense — how could the leg meridians possibly relate to frozen shoulder?" In fact, many skilled Chinese medicine practitioners know that numerous acupoints on the leg treat shoulder pain with remarkable effect.

For example: Tiaokou (ST-38) on the Stomach meridian, Jinmen (BL-63) on the Bladder meridian, Master Tung's Shenguan point (possibly relating to the Liver, Spleen, or Kidney meridians), and so on — all located on the leg. Thus abnormality of the leg meridians can also produce frozen shoulder.

Acupoints located on the leg can, astonishingly, also treat shoulder pain

All the leg meridians abnormal? That is no small matter! In Chinese medicine theory, the legs are the body's foundation; sickness of the leg meridians means the whole body is ill. Therefore, the real worry is not frozen shoulder, but the many more potential diseases lurking behind it.

A Cloud TCM member recalled that his friend Kevin developed frozen shoulder around 1997 — indeed at about age 50. Meridian assessment at the time revealed an "Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency" meridian pattern.

Besides being unable to raise his arm, Kevin also had the "three highs" (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia), mild gallstones, dry eye, sleep disturbance (waking easily at night), nocturia, chronic fatigue, generalized pain, and breathlessness climbing stairs — a truly sorry state.

At the time he tried tuina, acupuncture, and Chinese herbs at TCM clinics without clear effect, and also tried rehabilitation at a physiatry department with limited benefit. Finally he went to hospital for an injection. Kevin said at the time: "Really — after one injection in the shoulder, the pain was gone! Afterward I did rehabilitation exercises regularly, and within 1–2 years I forgot frozen shoulder existed."

For Kevin, the frozen shoulder had disappeared, but the other symptoms remained. Frozen shoulder, it turns out, was only the exposed tip of the iceberg, with unfathomable secrets of disease stored beneath. What truly demands attention is the enormous latent problem below.

Frozen shoulder is only the tip of the iceberg; the diseases hidden beneath the iceberg are the real point!

For modern medicine, what matters is that the arm no longer hurts and the shoulder can be raised — that is "recovery" or "cure." Hence modern medical treatment is uniform: one injection, immediate effect. But from the standpoint of Chinese medicine, it is not so simple.

To truly explore the causes of frozen shoulder from the Chinese-medicine angles of meridians, acupoints, sinew-channel and muscle adhesion, the six external pathogens, Zang-Fu Qi and Blood, and so on, one could write a thick book. Yet the modern person's formula of thought is: "Don't tell me all that — I have no time to listen. Just make the pain stop quickly so I can raise my arm!" So without further ado, an injection is of course fastest.

A wise person skilled in health cultivation who develops "frozen shoulder," if they will regularly observe and pat the relevant meridians (discussed below) to keep the meridians flowing, while diligently cultivating health so that these chaotic, severely abnormal meridians return to normal, can not only prevent recurrence of frozen shoulder but also prevent many major diseases.

As noted at the very beginning of this article, only 2–5% of people ever develop frozen shoulder. In other words, if a person begins health cultivation upon discovering Wind-Cold invasion or disharmony of the meridians and Zang-Fu, then besides avoiding the various chronic diseases (the three highs, heart disease, cancer, and so on), frozen shoulder becomes all the more impossible. Rather than studying how to use Chinese medicine to treat frozen shoulder, it is far more meaningful to study how to use Chinese medicine to prevent it.

The course runs through three phases: freezing (progressive pain and declining motion, roughly 6 weeks to 9 months), frozen (pain may ease but stiffness persists, roughly 4–6 months), and thawing (motion gradually returns, roughly 6 months to 2 years) — the full course can span 1 to 3 years.

"Fifty-year shoulder" is the popular term; modern medicine calls it "adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder." The shoulder joint capsule thickens and becomes fibrotic due to inflammation, synovial fluid decreases, joint function is impaired, adhesions form within the joint, and shoulder range of motion is compromised. The entire shoulder seems frozen in place, hence the alternative name "frozen shoulder."

Those who develop frozen shoulder suffer chronic shoulder pain, sharp pain when turning over in bed, restricted joint motion, inability to raise the arm or rotate it outward, difficulty lifting the hand high, and even trouble dressing — genuinely quite distressing.

According to Western research, roughly 2–5% of people worldwide develop this condition. Because onset occurs between 40 and 60 years of age — right around age 50 — it is called "fifty-year shoulder." The probability is thus actually quite low, and much shoulder joint pain is in fact not frozen shoulder.

To modern medicine, frozen shoulder is a rather mysterious disease: it arises spontaneously at a certain age, passes through three stages, and affects women more often than men. Scientists have tried blood tests, viral investigations, and analysis of aspirated joint fluid — and found nothing conclusive.

No matter how it is examined (X-ray, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, etc.), no major problem can be seen. Stranger still, most people gradually recover after a period of time (generally 1–3 years).

When the shoulder joint is injured, raising the arm produces pain.

Diabetic patients have a higher probability of developing frozen shoulder (prevalence up to 10%); patients with hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and hypertension also have elevated risk.

In most people, prolonged lack of shoulder movement leads to adhesions of the shoulder joint, which can also produce frozen shoulder. Rheumatoid arthritis and degenerative arthritis can likewise impair shoulder joint motion.

Chinese and Western medicine agree that frozen shoulder results from adhesion, inflammation, and fibrosis of the muscles around the shoulder — adhesions as frustrating as being stuck fast with super glue.

Treatments for frozen shoulder include anti-inflammatory medications (aspirin, corticosteroids, etc.) for relief; most commonly "physical therapy" (heat, electrotherapy) and "rehabilitation exercises." Some choose injection of sterile normal saline into the shoulder (hydrodilatation / capsular distension), and severe cases are managed surgically, for example with shoulder capsular release or distension arthroplasty.

From an anatomical standpoint, treating this disease is not difficult at all. Dr. Hsu Chia-lin, who has treated more than a thousand cases of frozen shoulder, states plainly in his book Save Your Own Shoulder Pain: "Frozen shoulder is really a very uninteresting minor disease — the joint capsule is stuck; just unstick it."

Since most of the time shoulder joint pain is not severe frozen shoulder and its cause is also unclear, such disorders of unknown cause are the most suitable for applying Chinese medicine theory — the pain may even be a signal of other disease, and it can be entirely prevented and healed on one's own, offering another new line of approach.

All six meridians passing through the knee can produce knee pain

Some people develop "anterior and lateral knee pain" after the weather turns cold in winter — this is the knee pain produced by the Gallbladder and Stomach meridian Deficiency commonly seen in winter, appearing especially readily in people of "Cold-type Yang-Deficient meridian constitution."

Knee pain is a common and complex pain. Some people develop knee pain on entering winter or summer, or when rain brings heavier dampness; the underlying causes are quite complex.

The painful site may involve the knee joint, the patella, sprained or torn ligaments, cartilage or other bony structures, or arthritis of the whole knee joint. There may be swelling and stiffness of the knee, redness and heat, weakness of the knee, strange noises from the knee, inability to fully straighten the knee, and so on.

Modern medicine recognizes many causes of knee pain — for example, obesity placing excessive pressure on the knee, or unsuitable footwear compressing and injuring the knee.

The most common knee pain is "degenerative arthritis" (osteoarthritis): with advancing age, the soft tissue within the knee joint wears down from overuse, and the knee becomes stiff and painful. "Gout," in which excess uric acid in the body causes inflammatory joint swelling and pain, is also a common cause of knee pain.

More serious is "rheumatoid arthritis," an autoimmune disease that most readily produces severe knee pain. In many cases, insufficient exercise leading to atrophy of the thigh muscles can also give rise to knee pain.

As for treatment, the usual advice is ample rest and avoidance of strenuous exercise, anti-inflammatory analgesics, nutritional supplements, and rehabilitative physical therapy. Severe cases may require intramuscular injection or artificial joint replacement surgery.

Since traditional Chinese medicine is also skilled at treating knee pain, for knee pain with no clearly identifiable cause, or milder knee pain, considering the perspective of the Chinese-medicine meridians to understand or improve the condition is a good option.

Knee pain can be broadly divided into anterior, lateral, medial, and posterior. What is discussed here is pain of the knee as a whole; for a specific region of the knee, click through to that region's page for deeper exploration.

Generalized body pain existed as a symptom a thousand years ago. The Han-dynasty Shanghan Lun already records names such as "body aching" and "generalized body pain." The Zhubing Yuanhou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Manifestations of Diseases), in its chapters on Wind disorders, states: "When Wind resides in the skin, there is a crawling, leaping sensation, as if scratching, as if pricking, with pain over the entire body..." — clearly the ancients experienced this pain.

Later Chinese medicine broadly advanced the concept of "Bi syndrome" (painful obstruction): a disease pattern in which external pathogens — Wind, Cold, Dampness, Heat — invade the body, block the meridians, and impede the circulation of Qi and Blood. Generalized body pain is closely bound to these causes.

Such Bi syndromes produce generalized soreness, numbness, heaviness, and impaired flexion and extension of the muscles, sinews, bones, and joints, even swollen, burning joints — so generalized aching pain never leaves this domain.

Since the external pathogens Wind, Cold, Dampness, and Heat cannot be verified by modern technology, nor can concepts like meridian Qi and Blood, they naturally cannot be detected by examination. Chinese medicine differentiates generalized body pain into the following patterns:

1. Sequelae of externally contracted Wind-Cold

The exterior pattern in Chinese medicine most often refers to "externally contracted Wind-Cold." During a cold, many people first feel generalized joint pain, aversion to cold with fever, nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, cough, and so on.

Verifying this generalized pain is easy: stay unclothed in an air-conditioned room until the whole body shivers, and it is readily confirmed. Yet these symptoms, properly belonging to a cold, can appear at ordinary times as well. The reasonable inference is that in some people, the Cold Damage of a cold never truly resolved, leaving behind this generalized Wind-Cold pain.

Since Cold is "Yin" in nature and erodes the body's Yang Qi, the long-retained imprint of Wind-Cold from colds, when examined by meridian assessment, most readily lodges as Deficiency patterns of the "Bladder meridian" and "Gallbladder meridian," becoming a long-term constitutional phenomenon.

The constitutional meridian phenomenon left behind by cold sequelae

Because the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians are highly interlinked, this ultimately becomes a pattern of Deficiency of all three leg Yang meridians; in some people even the three arm Yang meridians are simultaneously low in energy. One member once performed a meridian assessment for a friend with fibromyalgia and found precisely that these two meridians' energies were markedly low.

2. Externally contracted Wind-Cold-Damp pathogens

The Huangdi Neijing states: "When the three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together and combine, they form Bi." Beyond the Wind-Cold above, adding Dampness makes generalized pain even more likely. Taking "Wind pathogen" as the example: its hallmark is pain without fixed location — headache in the morning, low back pain in the afternoon. Taking "Cold pathogen": the pain is accompanied by a sensation of coldness, its location fixed, worsening as the temperature drops.

Dampness invading the body — from rain-soaking or an overly damp environment — also produces generalized pain, with accompanying symptoms such as heaviness of the limbs, head distension, a sensation of the head being wrapped in a towel, aversion to cold with fever, numbness of the skin, and dulled sensation.

So after the plum-rain season, typhoon days, getting caught in the rain for whatever reason, or swimming, hair-washing, saunas, and the like, one must dry the hair and body — otherwise, one day this strange generalized pain will begin.

3. Stasis and obstruction of the meridians

The meridians are like the body's rivers, needing periodic clearing and dredging to keep the flow smooth; otherwise, over time much refuse silts up. But modern people have no idea what meridians are, so they go a lifetime with no clearing plan; when the meridians' Qi and Blood have silted up with refuse long enough, pain begins.

Whichever meridian's Qi and Blood are obstructed, that meridian develops pain. The meridians most often obstructed in modern people are the Spleen, Bladder, and Gallbladder meridians. Open a chart of the body's meridians and acupoints and trace these three meridians' routes, and one discovers: "Is this not precisely generalized body pain?"

When a meridian is blocked, pain appears along that meridian

When a meridian is obstructed, sustained patting, gua sha, cupping, tuina, or massage along that meridian will naturally restore the flow of Qi and Blood — no doctor required, and the simplest of all health-cultivation methods.

Verifying the relationship between meridians and pain is easy, and anyone can experiment. A Cloud TCM member once shared a case: one summer, a relative had an electric fan blowing directly on the Gallbladder meridian of the calf and fell asleep in front of it, waking five hours later. From then on the calf hurt for 20 years, flaring whenever the weather turned cold.

4. Liver Qi stagnation

Chinese medicine holds that "the Liver stores Blood" and "the Liver governs the sinews." Modern people's tense lives, frequent setbacks at work, and chronic overwork readily produce Liver Qi stagnation, with impeded circulation of Qi and Blood and disharmony of Zang-Fu function. Observation by meridian assessment finds the most frequent presentation to be Liver meridian Excess with Spleen and Bladder meridian Deficiency — the meridian pattern most prone to generalized joint and muscle pain.

People with this meridian pattern often have depressed mood, insomnia at night, poor appetite, thirst, and dry mouth, and frequently develop all manner of gastrointestinal discomfort. Over time appear fatigue, weakness, a feeble voice, and emaciation or excessive obesity.

The Dampness mentioned above arises even more readily in such chronically Spleen-Deficient bodies, because the Spleen's capacity to transform and transport water is insufficient — hence generalized pain also appears.

5. Spleen Deficiency and dual Deficiency of Qi and Blood

Chinese medicine holds that "woman takes Blood as her foundation." Menstruation, pregnancy, and childbirth all deplete a woman's Yin-Blood; with the Qi and Blood of the channels insufficient and unable to nourish the sinews and bones, generalized pain ultimately results. This suffices to explain why women develop fibromyalgia more readily than men, and why the incidence of rheumatoid arthritis in women likewise exceeds that in men.

Meridian assessment finds Spleen and Kidney meridian Deficiency in large numbers of women, corroborating this fact. Women must therefore regularly apply Chinese-medicine concepts to nourish the Blood — a domain of knowledge missing from modern medicine.

Dual Deficiency of Qi and Blood has been the pattern-identification conclusion most habitual to Chinese medicine practitioners over the past thousand years, and Ba Zhen Tang (Eight Treasures Decoction) has been their favorite across those centuries, because most diseases clearly improve once Qi and Blood are tonified. Generalized pain of this origin is the most suitable for tonifying Qi and Blood.[@post:388]

6. Yang-Deficient constitution (Kidney Yang Deficiency)

Chinese medicine holds that the Kidney is the root of the earlier heaven (congenital constitution), storing Essence and governing bone, while the Spleen is the root of the later heaven (acquired constitution), the source of the body's Qi and Blood, closely bound to the muscles and four limbs. As noted above, meridian assessment finds Spleen and Kidney meridian Deficiency in large numbers of women — this is the chief reason women readily develop fibromyalgia.

Kidney Deficiency is often produced by excessive internal Cold. Large volumes of meridian data show that Kidney meridian Deficiency is frequently accompanied by Gallbladder and Stomach meridian Deficiency, a meridian pattern to which women are especially prone — hence most women have cold hands and feet and constant fatigue.

The meridian pattern in which women readily develop generalized body pain

One member shared that several years ago he met a Western woman with pain throughout her body who had never in her life taken Chinese medicine. He assessed her meridians and found precisely Gallbladder, Stomach, and Kidney meridian Deficiency. Modern medicine has defined a term for generalized, body-wide pain: "fibromyalgia." It is a mysterious pain disorder that is difficult to comprehend. Patients often complain of pain all over the body, yet a battery of examinations frequently fails to find a cause.

Patients present with widespread pain throughout the body, while the muscle tissue shows no pathological change. This pain is frequently accompanied by many other symptoms, for example: cognitive impairment, chronic fatigue syndrome, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, exhaustion and weakness, headache, temporomandibular joint pain, numbness and pain of the hands and feet, irritable bowel syndrome, forgetfulness, inability to concentrate, dysmenorrhea, and so on.

Because the cause of this disease is unknown, there is also no specific test to confirm the diagnosis. It affects women more than men, with peak onset in women aged 30–40, so it is sometimes called the "princess disease." Modern medicine speculates it may be related to nutrient deficiencies, for example: magnesium, selenium, taurine, melatonin, superoxide dismutase, and so on.

Not only is the cause unknown, but treatment with ordinary analgesics is also poorly effective. Because patients frequently present with anxiety or depression, many physicians regard the condition as a psychiatric disorder, and accordingly quite a few psychotropic drugs have been employed to treat it.

A disease like this — of unknown cause and with no established treatment — is actually the most suitable for approaching through Chinese medicine, because Chinese-medicine theory provides levels of analysis that modern medicine lacks.

Headache is a symptom that has troubled the Chinese people for thousands of years, so Traditional Chinese Medicine has extremely rich experience in treating headache. TCM approaches headache from both its 'cause' and its 'location.' TCM holds that the causes of headache, as with other diseases, are divided into 'external contraction' and 'internal damage.'

TCM theory frequently mentions the concept of the so-called 'Six Pathogens,' which refers to 'Wind, Cold, Summerheat, Dampness, Dryness, and Fire' — six kinds of natural Qi, also called the 'six externally contracted excesses (Liu Yin).' This concept is of external origin, somewhat like what modern people commonly call catching a cold.

When the body is invaded by the externally contracted 'Six Pathogens' (Wind, Cold, Summerheat, Dampness, Dryness, Fire), the movement of Qi and Blood in the head becomes obstructed and headache appears; the most common headaches are mainly those caused by 'Wind-Cold,' 'Wind-Heat,' and 'Wind-Dampness.'

All of the external Six Pathogens can cause headache/migraine.

Because 'Wind' invading the body causes headache, and 'Cold' invading the body also causes headache, a headache caused by [Wind + Cold] is a 'Wind-Cold headache' — one headache pattern. Reasoning by analogy, many, many patterns arise, and every pattern has its corresponding Chinese herbal formula.

Headache from internal damage is mostly long-standing chronic pain, usually caused by internal damage to the Zang-Fu organs, Qi and Blood insufficient to nourish, and turbid Phlegm and static Blood obstructing the meridians. On this basis, the TCM patterns of headache are extremely numerous.

According to the current records of the Cloud TCM database, there are more than 1,400 Chinese herbal formulas that can treat headache — many people wanting to learn Chinese medicine would probably start getting a headache upon seeing this number?!

Only through database technology does one learn that the Chinese herbs able to treat headache are astonishingly numerous.

From the meridian perspective, the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) states: 'The head is the mansion of clear brightness.' The Qi and Blood of all Five Zang and Six Fu organs, the twelve meridians, and the Eight Extraordinary Vessels pour upward into the head; therefore the head is the meeting place of all the Yang, and also the meeting place of all the Yin!

After external pathogens invade the body, they cause abnormal movement of Qi and Blood in the meridians; whichever meridian is abnormal, the pain appears at a different location. Therefore, the ancients often diagnosed the cause of headache according to its location; the common classifications are as follows:

1. Taiyang headache

This type of headache mostly occurs at the back of the head, extending down to the neck and back. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Taiyang Bladder meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'tension (stress) headache,' and here it can also be identified as 'occipital headache.'

This type of headache accounts for the highest proportion and tends to occur in people with heavy work stress, emotional tension, or overwork, so its causes are related to emotions and stress. It usually strikes from afternoon into evening, and the greater the stress and the tenser the emotions (nervousness, anger, agitation, anxiety, depression, etc.), the more intense the headache becomes.

Meridian examination can completely prove this: anyone under heavy stress and fatigue has an extremely high probability of showing the so-called 'Iron Triangle meridian pattern,' in which Bladder meridian energy is extremely low, so occipital headache readily appears. Moreover, the Bladder meridian is active in the afternoon, so headache readily occurs in the afternoon.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern most readily produces headache.

More attentive observers will also notice that in this meridian pattern the Spleen meridian also shows Deficiency, which is why modern medicine also finds that this type of headache is accompanied by poor appetite.[@ad:1]

2. Jueyin headache

The so-called Jueyin headache is vertex headache, commonly at the crown of the head, and may extend to the eyes. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Jueyin Liver meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it also corresponds to 'tension (stress) headache.'

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern above can substantiate Jueyin headache: because of Liver meridian Excess, pain appears at the vertex. Cloud TCM member Mr. K once shared that his meridian pattern was of this type and he also had frequent headaches; he found that practicing relaxation and going to sleep a little earlier could improve this meridian pattern, and the headaches that came with it would disappear as well!

3. Yangming headache

This type of headache mostly occurs at the forehead and causes supraorbital ridge (brow bone) pain. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Yangming Stomach meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'cluster headache.' From large volumes of meridian data on modern people, the meridian pattern common in men very readily produces frontal headache and pain in the eye socket and supraorbital ridge.

The meridian pattern in which Yangming headache appears.

The meridian pattern common in women, meanwhile, very readily causes headaches along the pathways of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians.

The meridian pattern common in women readily causes frontal headache and migraine.

4. Shaoyang headache

This type of headache commonly appears on both sides of the head, the neck and shoulders, and the ear region. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Shaoyang Gallbladder meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'migraine,' appearing most often in women — and the meridian phenomena in the figure above decode the reason behind it.

The Gallbladder meridian spreads over the entire side of the head.

A certain Cloud TCM member, Ms. S, observed the meridian phenomena causing her headaches over a period of as long as 8 years. She had chronic Gallbladder meridian Deficiency, the same whether in winter or summer, with the Stomach and Kidney meridians also frequently Deficient — this is the 'Yang Deficiency' meridian phenomenon often mentioned in Cloud TCM articles.

The meridian chart also reveals the phenomena of Wind-Cold headache and Kidney-Deficiency headache.

When winter arrived, she would very readily develop headache, runny nose, and sneezing — this is the 'Wind-Cold headache' caused by Cold Qi; and because Cold damages the Kidney, her Kidney meridian was frequently Deficient, so it could also be called a 'Kidney-Deficiency headache.'

Each time she encountered this phenomenon, she took 'Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang (Ephedra, Aconite, and Asarum Decoction),' which rapidly improved all her symptoms, and the headache quickly disappeared. For those who wish to understand in depth: if you study this herbal formula carefully, you will know it is a formula that dispels (Cold Damage) Wind-Cold and boosts Kidney energy and Yang Qi, so it perfectly matches this pattern.

Based on the four points above, the causes behind 'primary headache,' so intractable to modern medicine, are completely decoded by meridian theory. Since this article discusses simple headache, click 'Migraine,' 'Vertex headache,' or 'Occipital headache' for a deeper understanding.

In fact, treating headache is very complex — the acupoints that can improve headache are numerous enough to give one a headache. Just how many acupoints in the human body can treat headache? In the past, no one could fully clarify this, because the complete acupoint lists a human brain can memorize are actually few. Now, through the integration of computer software technology, in the Cloud TCM meridian-acupoint database alone there are as many as 140 or more regular-meridian acupoints that can treat headache.

Every meridian carries acupoints that can improve headache (migraine).

If these acupoints that can improve headache (migraine) are classified by meridian into a pie chart, one finds 30 on the Gallbladder meridian, 29 on the Bladder meridian, 19 on the Triple Burner meridian, 13 on the Governing Vessel, 11 on the Small Intestine meridian, 10 on the Large Intestine meridian, and so on.

The acupoint lists generated by data-analysis technology have completely decoded a millennium of acupoint indications and effects. Taking this headache article as an example, as long as you have performed meridian examinations over the long term, you can see acupoint recommendations that belong entirely to you.

Facing the most common headaches, patting the entire Bladder meridian (back, buttocks, backs of the knees, backs of the calves) and the Gallbladder meridian (outer thighs) can relieve the greater part. Alternatively, warming these two meridians with moxibustion, heat therapy, or far-infrared therapy can also improve ordinary primary headache.

Migraine, too, is a symptom that has troubled the Chinese people for over a thousand years, so similar names in the ancient classics are numerous. This type of headache is often rather stubborn and not quickly cured; its treatment can be explored together with general 'headache.'

If one holds a bronze acupuncture figure in hand, one can clearly see that the head is mainly influenced by the Bladder meridian, while the meridian mainly influencing the side of the head is the 'Gallbladder meridian.' However, meridians such as the Triple Burner, Small Intestine, Large Intestine, and Stomach meridians all exert influence as well.

The Gallbladder meridian spreads over the entire side of the head.

The ancient text Lan Shi Mi Cang (Secrets from the Orchid Chamber) states: 'For pain in half the head, first choose the Hand Shaoyang and Yangming, then choose the Foot Shaoyang and Yangming — this is hemilateral headache (migraine).' The meaning of this passage is that headache is intimately related to the Gallbladder, Triple Burner, Large Intestine, and Stomach meridians.

After long-term observation through meridian examination, Cloud TCM members found that migraine is indeed closely related to these 4 meridians, described separately below:

1. Shaoyang meridian (Gallbladder and Triple Burner) abnormality

In modern people, the Gallbladder meridian shows Deficiency in all four seasons, with a probability stably above 70%, higher in women than in men. The Triple Burner meridian shows Excess in all four seasons, with a probability likewise stably at 60-70% or above. It can therefore be said that modern people's Shaoyang meridians are perpetually in an unbalanced, uncoordinated state.

Modern people's Shaoyang meridians (Gallbladder and Triple Burner) are chronically unbalanced.

If a person's Gallbladder meridian remains severely Deficient over the long term while the Triple Burner meridian is severely Excess, then they truly can hardly escape the fate of migraine. The probability of attacks was especially high in winter. These are all typical symptoms of Gallbladder and Triple Burner meridian abnormality.

When Yangming is abnormal, there may be impaired sense of smell, facial muscle abnormalities, neck and shoulder soreness, soreness of the elbow and the upper and lower arm, eye abnormalities, various symptoms of the Spleen-Stomach digestive tract (constipation, diarrhea, poor appetite, persistent hunger, etc.), vertigo, confused speech, and so on — all typical Yangming meridian symptoms.

3. Combined variants of the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians

The above merely discusses the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians separately; in fact, on a single meridian chart they appear together. The linkage between the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians is very strong — that is, when the Gallbladder meridian is Deficient, the Stomach meridian is Deficient in tandem — and the same holds for the Triple Burner and Large Intestine meridians, so the following two possibilities appear.

Common meridian patterns of the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians.

This is caused by depressed mood, with Liver Qi constrained in the body for a long time until it transforms into Fire.

The Liver-Yang-rising meridian pattern very readily produces migraine.

Some members have indeed observed this meridian phenomenon: it is the typical Iron Triangle meridian phenomenon, plus Excess of the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians (as in the figure above). This truly can produce migraine, with a higher probability of appearing in summer, together with the series of Liver-Yang-rising symptoms — everyone can verify this for themselves.

Whatever the meridian pattern, as long as the body's meridians are chronically obstructed, producing Qi stagnation and Blood stasis within the body, migraine can appear — because the meridians in which the human body most readily develops Qi-Blood stasis are the Bladder and Gallbladder meridians, and both of these meridians pass through the head.

From the above it can be seen that external Cold most readily causes migraine, which is why migraine appears most readily in winter. Applying 'moxibustion,' a 'hot hair dryer,' or 'far-infrared irradiation' to the head and the related meridian areas, or a lower-body hot bath, patting the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians, and warming the navel, are the fastest and simplest methods to improve migraine.

Arthritis is a disease with a very long history — there is evidence of osteoarthritis dating as far back as the age of the dinosaurs, and arthritis is often considered the most common disease of prehistoric humans; both 'Otzi the Iceman' (c. 3000 BCE) and Egyptian mummies (c. 2590 BCE) show arthritis on their bodies.

It is therefore no surprise that Chinese medicine began treating arthritis in remote antiquity, and similar disease names are quite numerous. The most frequently used names are the 'Li Jie pain (joint-running pain)' recorded in the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage) and the 'Bi syndrome (impediment syndrome)' discussed in the Huangdi Neijing. The Su Wen chapter 'On Bi' states: 'When the three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together and combine, they form Bi' — evidently the ancients held that arthritis is mainly caused by Wind, Cold, and Dampness.

1. Wind-Cold invading the body

As mentioned above, Wind, Cold, and Dampness are the main causes of 'Bi syndrome'; here we first discuss Wind-Cold. The ancient text Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (On the Origins and Manifestations of Diseases) says: 'The Wind pathogen moves with the Qi'; the Sheng Ji Zong Lu (Comprehensive Records of Sagely Benefaction) says: 'Wind is Yang Qi; it moves readily and changes frequently.'

The 'Wind' spoken of in Chinese medicine is an abstract concept: once it enters the body, the phenomenon of pain wandering from place to place appears, so it is also called 'migratory Bi (Xing Bi).' The ancients held that pure Wind could be addressed with the treatment method of tonifying Blood, because 'to treat Wind, first treat the Blood; when the Blood moves, the Wind extinguishes of itself.'

Most of the time, however, 'Wind' and 'Cold Qi' operate together, and then the Cold Qi must also be dispelled. Since Cold governs congealing and stagnation, the location of the pain does not change, the limbs are ice-cold, it worsens when the weather is cold, and warming the limbs with heat brings relief.

This Wind-Cold arthritis quite obviously worsens when the weather turns cold, so the cause can be observed directly in the meridian phenomena when the weather turns cold. Since Cold is a Yin Qi that erodes the energy of the Yang meridians in winter, the following meridian pattern appears when winter arrives, and joint pain appears most readily.

The Yang-Deficient meridian pattern readily produces arthritis.

In November 2021, Taiwan had an early cold snap with frequent continuous overcast rain. A member, Ms. K, found that all the joints of her hands became painful — more painful when making a fist — and in addition there was knee pain, low back pain, buttock pain, toe pain, and so on: almost her whole body was in pain, with nocturia more than 8 times a night — extremely distressing. Her meridian examination was just like this pattern: Deficiency of the three Foot Yang meridians and Deficiency of the Kidney meridian.

2. Cold-Dampness invading the body

Wind-Cold is usually also accompanied by Dampness. Taking the Taiwan region as an example, cold fronts are usually accompanied by rainy days, so Wind, Cold, and Dampness usually exist together and are not easily separated — which is why the ancients said 'the three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together and combine to form Bi.'

The 'Dampness pathogen,' like the 'Cold pathogen,' is very difficult to drive out: the pain is fixed and unchanging, and it may even cause numbness and insensitivity of the skin, stubbornly rigid muscles, and deformity of the joints. Since Cold and Dampness are both Yin pathogens, they erode the energy of the body's Yang meridians; therefore, when overcast, rainy weather arrives, meridian examination can be used to prove this phenomenon.

Yang meridians without energy mean that the body's Small Intestine, Large Intestine, Triple Burner, Gallbladder, Stomach, and Bladder meridians lack energy — Qi and Blood insufficiency. Readers may consult the meridian charts for themselves: pain can appear anywhere these meridians pass, which indeed amounts to 'no place in the body without pain.'

The ancients used the method of 'warming Yang and transforming Dampness' to make the Cold Qi and Dampness leave the body. With ample Yang Qi in the body's meridians, circulation naturally flows freely, and any arthritis causing pain automatically disappears — this is the basic principle by which the ancients treated arthritis.

3. Damp-Heat invading the body

The above mentions that Wind-Cold-Damp causes Bi syndrome — so can 'Heat' cause Bi syndrome? The ancients found that it can!

This Heat usually occurs in summer, and since the dominant Qi of summer is Dampness, Damp-Heat usually appears together. Besides pain in the joints of the limbs, there are symptoms such as fever, thirst, restlessness, a red tongue with a yellow dry coating, a rapid pulse, and so on.

Since these are the main symptoms of summer, simply observing the meridian phenomena that most commonly appear in summer clearly reveals that they are caused by the 'Iron Triangle meridian pattern' and its variants. In summer there is a high probability of Liver meridian Excess with Spleen and Bladder meridian Deficiency; if Dampness is combined with this, arthritis very readily appears.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern and its variants readily produce arthritis.

Have readers ever wondered why gout always appears at the big toe? Is the big toe not precisely the starting point of the Liver and Spleen meridians?! Modern medicine finds that stress and overwork bring on gout, and many members have already experimented personally: merely staying up late for more than three days makes the meridian pattern naturally display the Iron Triangle.

Gout readily appears in men, the obese, hypertensive patients, and diabetic patients — and these people are the most likely to show the Iron Triangle meridian pattern. This meridian pattern is also the typical 'Liver Qi constraint' pattern, which over time transforms into Heat within the body, as can be clearly seen from its variant form.

4. Whole-body Qi stagnation and Blood stasis; obstructed meridians

As noted above, most people's arthritis is caused by Wind, Cold, Dampness, and Heat in the body — and in the great majority of people, they all come at once! That is, the body harbors an extremely complex situation, which finally becomes very difficult to treat. This is the end result molded through every stage of life without correct health cultivation.

Judging from the constitutions of most modern people, the body ordinarily harbors latent Heat, and then externally contracts Wind-Cold-Damp, producing the various Bi syndromes. The ancient text Jin Kui Yi (Supplement to the Golden Cabinet) had already observed this phenomenon: 'The Fu and Zang organs and meridians first harbor accumulated Heat, and then Wind, Cold, and Damp Qi lodge there; the Heat is constrained by the Cold, the Qi cannot flow through, and over time the Cold too transforms into Heat, and there is Bi with oppression.'

The final result of this phenomenon is whole-body Qi stagnation and Blood stasis, with the Qi and Blood of the meridians entirely blocked: whichever meridian is severely obstructed, that meridian will manifest pain! Since modern medicine does not know what the meridians are, the cause usually cannot be found.

Patting the meridians by following the charts is actually very simple.

The best method at this point is whole-body meridian patting — first unblock the meridians of one's entire body — and one may also combine this with some Chinese herbs or foods that open the meridians and tonify Qi and Blood; this can be called the first step in solving a complex problem. As for precisely which meridians to pat: simply use meridian examination, and diligently pat whichever ones show red — very simple.

5. Liver and Kidney depletion

Liver-Kidney depletion is almost the pattern most commonly diagnosed by TCM physicians when middle-aged and elderly people seek TCM treatment. The reason is simple: as the sayings go, 'the Liver governs the sinews' and 'the Kidney governs the bones'; when the Liver and Kidney are depleted, the sinews and bones of the whole body lose nourishment and become painful.

Since the middle-aged and elderly, and those past menopause, all present a state of Liver-Kidney Qi and Blood insufficiency, they most readily develop generalized aching of the sinews and bones — completely consistent with the data observed by modern medicine.

What symptoms does Liver-Kidney depletion produce? Common ones include: slack, tight, or aching sinews and bones, vertigo, withered and brittle nails, soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees, tinnitus, deafness, loose teeth, hair loss, impotence, seminal emission, pain of the joints of the limbs, and so on.

The aging process is the summation of Yang Deficiency plus the Iron Triangle meridian pattern.

What exactly is Liver-Kidney depletion? It can be learned by observing the meridian patterns of the elderly. Most people begin showing the 'Yang Deficiency' and 'Iron Triangle' meridian phenomena from young adulthood, only unstably. In old age, these two meridian patterns combine and become stable and unchanging, forming the 'Excess above, Deficiency below' meridian pattern.

From the chart it can be clearly seen that the energy of the feet and legs is completely insufficient — how could foot pain possibly not appear? Therefore, health cultivation for the middle-aged and elderly must tonify and nourish the Liver and Kidney, improving the body's state of 'Excess above, Deficiency below'; in this way one's sinews and bones can function normally, and only then will the legs have strength!
